units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Where are we?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You're on North Michigan Avenue, outside the building you're staying in.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Cross the street if you can, and look up.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: This is the Carbide and Carbon Building, finished in 1929.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Wait. I just slept in a landmark?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You'll sleep in one tonight. It was built for a company called Union Carbide and Carbon, and the architects were the Burnham Brothers, the sons of the famous planner Daniel Burnham.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Famous planner. You always say that like I'm supposed to know him.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You will by the end of the walk.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now look at the colors. The base is polished black granite, with black marble and bronze trim.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The tall middle part is dark green and gold terra cotta.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the top is trimmed in gold leaf.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Real gold?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Twenty-four karat. The building's own history says the architects looked at imitation gold and rejected it.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A gold hat on a green skyscraper.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Bold.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Here's the story everyone tells.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That it was designed to look like a dark green champagne bottle with gold foil on the top.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh, I love that.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a legend. A popular one, going back to the 1920s, but the designers never said so.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The documented story is better.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The leaf patterns refer to how carbon forms from ancient plants that decayed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the letter C appears again and again, because of the company name.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So it's a building about coal.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: In gold.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Carbon, yes. Roughly. The company's ground floor was a showroom for its products.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A showroom. For skyscraper-sized carbon.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Look at the top again. Since 2007 the gold crown has been lit every night, which helped the champagne story along.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The building is five hundred and three feet tall, thirty-seven floors, and Chicago made it a landmark in 1996.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then it became a hotel.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Eventually. A hotel opened in it in 2004.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It closed and reopened more than once.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then in 2020 a new owner bought it, and the Pendry opened in 2021.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I notice you said "more than once," in a very careful voice.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a landmark with a complicated career.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The lobby has Belgian marble and frosted glass light fixtures, if you want a look on the way out.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Let's go. Which way?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Walk north on Michigan Avenue, toward the river.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's about a three-minute walk, and the bridge is right in front of you.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Teaser?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We'll get there.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I knew you'd say that.
